world_change.statement: Persistent Strait of Hormuz disruption has reconfigured fertilizer supply chains, with severe initial disruption followed by uneven adaptation.

nodes.statement: Fertilizer trade and inputs through the Gulf/Hormuz system were severely disrupted in 2026.

provenance.locator: 24 Sep 2026 statement: Gulf shares, delayed fertilizer trade, Hormuz tanker movements
Fertilizers chapter: export disruption and March price surge

nodes.limitations: Does not establish equal impact in every fertilizer or destination.
nodes.geography: Strait of Hormuz / Persian Gulf / global

nodes.statement: Gulf supply concentration is material for urea, ammonia and sulfur and Hormuz carries a material share of traded fertilizer.

provenance.locator: Gulf supplies 30-35% global urea, 50% sulfur exports, 20-30% ammonia; Hormuz 20-30% traded fertilizer

nodes.limitations: Shares vary by product and measurement period.

nodes.statement: The initial disruption sharply raised fertilizer prices, especially urea.

provenance.locator: April urea above $850/mt, up 80% since February

nodes.limitations: Market prices do not prove local farm-gate prices or fertilizer non-use.

nodes.statement: By September nitrogen markets had partly adapted, while phosphate remained tight and sulfur was a major bottleneck.

provenance.locator: Key takeaways: nitrogen returning toward pre-war levels; phosphate tight; sulfur bottleneck

nodes.limitations: Adaptation is uneven across products and countries.

nodes.statement: Bangladesh is highly fertilizer-import dependent and received emergency financing to secure fertilizer for Aman and Boro rice seasons.

provenance.locator: Imports >85% fertilizer requirements; 600,000t financing; 1.4m ha smallholder rice; Aman+Boro ~90% rice

nodes.limitations: Financing and exposure do not prove realized crop losses.

nodes.statement: Bangladesh continued large-scale procurement and district allocation to maintain supply.

provenance.locator: 110,000t approved from Belarus, Morocco, Saudi Arabia
100% October TSP/DAP/MOP allocation against demand in all 64 districts

nodes.limitations: Official procurement/allocation records do not independently prove last-mile delivery to every farmer.

nodes.statement: Bangladesh reported adequate or surplus national fertilizer stocks by August-September.

provenance.locator: Agriculture Secretary: no current fertilizer shortage; adequate stocks
51.71 lakh tonnes prepared supply vs 35.87 lakh tonnes demand; 15.84 lakh tonne surplus

nodes.limitations: National aggregate stocks may not describe every local market or timing issue.

nodes.statement: Australia was highly exposed to Middle East fertilizer supply and used targeted price-risk support and alternative sourcing.

provenance.locator: Australia entirely import reliant for urea; 62% fertilizer imports from Middle East

nodes.limitations: Exposure did not become a sustained national shortage.

nodes.statement: By August Australian urea arrivals exceeded estimated seasonal demand.

provenance.locator: Urea arrivals surpassed estimated seasonal demand

nodes.limitations: Demand estimates can change with planting and rainfall.

nodes.statement: The degree to which individual Bangladesh smallholders experienced higher farm-gate fertilizer prices, delayed access, reduced application or yield effects is not established by the current evidence pack.
A direct household food-price effect attributable specifically to the fertilizer shock is not established.
nodes.limitations: Food prices have multiple drivers and fertilizer effects can lag.

nodes.statement: Forecasts of future fertilizer, crop-yield or food-security effects remain conditional rather than observed outcomes.
nodes.limitations: Forecast assumptions can fail as shipping, production and policy change.

edges.relation: supply concentration increases exposure to chokepoint disruption
edges.boundary: Supports structural exposure, not uniform country-level shortage.

edges.relation: trade/production disruption contributed to initial fertilizer price surge
edges.boundary: Other energy, production and policy factors also affected prices.

edges.relation: markets adapted over time while some input constraints persisted
edges.boundary: Do not describe adaptation as full normalization.

edges.relation: global fertilizer shock created import-financing risk for Bangladesh
edges.boundary: Emergency action mitigated risk; it is not evidence of realized crop failure.

edges.relation: import dependence and seasonal needs prompted procurement/allocation response
edges.boundary: Procurement response does not prove perfect local distribution.

edges.relation: procurement, stocks and allocation are consistent with maintained national availability
edges.boundary: Do not claim these actions alone caused all stock sufficiency.

edges.relation: national sufficiency leaves local access effects unresolved
fertilizer price pressure may contribute to later food-price pressure
edges.boundary: No direct household food-price attribution without additional evidence.

edges.relation: Middle East disruption exposed Australia's import dependence and triggered supply response
edges.boundary: Response prevented a simple shortage narrative.

edges.relation: supply response coincided with arrivals exceeding estimated seasonal demand
edges.boundary: Do not assign sole causality to the government facility.
